news.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles, adding to streak of weapons tests
news.text:
North Korea on Monday fired multiple ballistic missiles toward its eastern waters, South Korea’s military said, adding to a recent streak of weapons demonstrations that has heightened tensions during a prolonged freeze in diplomacy.

Jang Do-young, spokesperson of South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, said missiles of various types were fired from an area around the North Korean capital of Pyongyang, where the country’s main airport has been a major launch site in recent years.

Jang said one of the missiles flew more than 559 miles before falling into the sea but didn’t comment on the flight details of the other weapons. The joint chiefs didn’t specify how many missiles it detected.

Japan’s Defense Ministry said it detected at least two missiles and that the weapons landed in waters outside the country’s exclusive economic zone. Japan’s prime minister’s office said no damage has been reported.

While maintaining a hard line toward Seoul, North Korea has been ramping up weapons testing as it seeks to expand its arsenal of nuclear-capable systems, including an Oct. 3 test of what the North described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defenses in South Korea and Japan.

North Korea has also conducted other missile tests and live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship as leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons program while rejecting US and South Korean offers to resume long-stalled diplomacy.

The latest launch came days after South Korea on Friday flight-tested its own domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defense systems, which President Lee Jae Myung described as critical in strengthening the South’s conventional defense capabilities.

Without directly addressing the growing threat from North Korea, Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theater of operations.”

Jang, the South Korean military official, said the latest North Korean launches likely were intended to advance the country’s missile technologies while also serving as a possible response to South Korea’s hypersonic test.

He declined to say whether the military assessed that the North had further tested its hypersonic technologies in the latest launch, saying the event was still being analyzed.

The South’s presidential national security office called for North Korea to “immediately cease” its repeated ballistic launches, which violate UN Security Council resolutions against the North and “do not help manage the current situation on the Korean Peninsula.”

Tensions were further worsened after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border. The South’s military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South’s demands for an apology.

Kim in recent years has halted all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and described the neighbor as a permanent enemy during a prolonged stalemate in larger nuclear negotiations with Washington.

He has so far rebuffed US President Donald Trump’s calls to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearization as a precondition for talks.

news.text:

During an apperance Sunday on NBC's Meet the Press with Kristen Welker, the senator warned that the president's deal could possibly violate the 2022 law passed by Congress that bans Russian oil imports unless specific conditions were met, including the country's withdrawal from Ukraine.

"I do believe there's a legitimate case for saying the president's not following the law," Tillis explained. "We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of the territory they occupied."

When Politico reached out to the White House for comment, they were directed to a Truth Social post from the president declaring an energy ceasefire. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," posted the president.

"Both parties have agreed," Trump added. "Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP." The president's post did not provide any details on the ceasefire nor any evidence that Russia had agreed to the deal.

Trump's post followed an ABC's "This Week" interview with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who called on the president to support the ceasefire. The president also announced on Friday that Russia would "immediately supply" diesel fuel to global markets in an effort to relieve some of the high prices at the pump due to the Iran war.

On Saturday, the president defended the U.S.'s actions in Iran and demanded an end to Ukraine's drone strikes that have crippled Russian oil refineries.

"These are bad people hanging out with bad people, putting American lives at risk — particularly our Special Operators and forward-deployed personnel," Tillis worried. He added, "I guarantee you, at the first opportunity Putin has to embarrass or undermine President Trump, he will." The president's announcement is a sharp pivot from the sanctions signed into law last month.

The legislation, which had been championed by the late senator Lindsey Graham, was meant to deplete Moscow's resources by targeting Russian officials, banks, and a shadow fleet of oil tankers. Both Democrats and Republicans supported the bill in both the House and the Senate.

According to Tillis, the president's actions were "tarnishing" the legacy of Graham. In the president's ever-shifting rhetoric, Trump also demanded that the country hold an election, something Tillis cautioned the president over.

"The president needs to realize that tens of thousands of people have died over this illegal invasion, and I get it that he may be frustrated," said Tillis. "But he needs to understand who the good guys are in this disagreement and who the bad guys are, and it's not even close."

news.title: Dollar stays near 18-month high as Mideast conflict, inflation data in focus
news.text:
Business News and FinanceVIEW IN APPMarketsBusinessInvestingTechPoliticsSelectMake ItCurrenciesDollar stays near 18-month high as Mideast conflict, inflation data in focusPublished Mon, Oct 12 2026 12:06 AM EDTReutersWATCH LIVEIn this article

The dollar held ground near its strongest level in a year and a half in early Asian trade on Monday as an escalating Middle East conflict kept investors wary ahead of key US inflation data later this week that will influence monetary policy.

Oil prices swung between gains and losses after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis stepped up strikes on Saudi Arabia while two tankers were attacked over the weekend.

Prices were also influenced by Sunday's announcement from US President Donald Trump about an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. Brent crude futures were down 1% at $103.55 per barrel in Asian hours.

The dollar index, which measures the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was slightly down at 102.14 but remained not far from the 18-month peak it scaled last week. Trading was confined to a tight range with Japanese markets shut for a holiday, thinning liquidity across the region.

"We expect the Houthis to continue their attacks on Saudi Arabian energy assets, supporting gains in the oil price and the USD," analysts at Commonwealth Bank of Australia said in a note.

They added that while Iran had confirmed receiving a US peace proposal through intermediaries, "we do not expect a breakthrough this week."

Against the yen, the US dollar was down 0.14% at 158.160 yen. The Australian dollar and its kiwi counterpart were both roughly flat at $0.6988 and $0.5614, respectively.

Beyond the geopolitical backdrop, the market's focus turns to Wednesday's US consumer price index report, one of the last major economic releases before the Federal Reserve's late-October meeting on interest rates.

Data last week showed U.S. consumer sentiment slumped further in early October as the rising cost of living because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy.

The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023 to rein in inflation, with markets keeping a close watch on economic data to gauge whether policymakers may move again. Traders are pricing in an 81% chance of the Fed standing pat this month, up from 51% a month earlier, CME FedWatch tool showed.

Even otherwise, the dollar's rally may be due for a pause in the near term with some pullback possible, Barclays analysts said.

They said sharp moves in bond markets had tightened global financial conditions, which could prompt Fed officials to strike a more reassuring tone heading into the October meeting, particularly if the CPI reading comes in soft.

Severe selloffs in bond markets in the past few weeks had left investors worried as borrowing costs across the globe rose to multi-decade highs on worries over inflation, energy prices and ballooning government debt.

The euro was up nearly 0.1% at $1.121, after clocking a fifth straight week of losses as the common currency bore the brunt of investor angst around France's fiscal health amid political uncertainty before the 2027 presidential election.

"It is still too early to tell whether higher borrowing costs will be sufficient to impose greater fiscal discipline on the French government," said OCBC FX strategists.

"We expect EURUSD to consolidate as the intensity of French fiscal and political headlines is unlikely to be sustained," they said in a note, adding any rally in the euro is likely to be capped by Europe's structural challenges.

The British pound was little changed at $1.3245. Against the Chinese yuan, the US dollar was flat at 6.6927 yuan in offshore trade.

In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin rose 0.2% to $83,788.50, while ether edged 0.15% up to $2,540.08.

news.title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Zelensky says Putin struck power plant hours after Trump ‘ceasefire’ announcement
news.text:
Volodymyr Zelensky has said Ukraine will support a bilateral “energy ceasefire” with Russia, after being caught off guard by Donald Trump’s shock announcement that a deal had already been agreed.

In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, the US president said: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”

The Ukrainian president said he had not heard of such a deal, but would agree to it if Russia did, according to Axios. Kyiv had publicly backed a truce on striking energy infrastructure before Trump announced on Friday plans to lift sanctions on Moscow to supply diesel to the US and global markets - much to Zelensky’s chagrin.

The Kremlin is still yet to acknowledge Trump’s claim to have established a ceasefire between the warring sides. Russia had reportedly sought sanctions relief as a concession for its adherence to a ceasefire earlier in the week.

The controversial diesel deal with Russia has proven controversial even within Trump’s own base as the president looks to bring down energy prices in the US ahead of the November midterm elections.

Trump hit out at Zelensky on Saturday, saying it was time for Ukraine to find a new leader after Kyiv struck Russian oil refineries. Zelensky said on Sunday he would hold new elections if Putin agrees to a 60-day “total ceasefire”.

news.title: US judge blocks taxpayer-funded Trump ads
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 12 (IANS) A federal judge has ordered President Donald Trump's administration to immediately stop airing taxpayer-funded television advertisements promoting President Donald Trump, handing a legal victory to groups challenging the use of government money for political messaging weeks before the November midterm elections. US District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York on Sunday (local time) issued a temporary restraining order barring the administration from developing, placing or broadcasting the disputed advertisements for 14 days. The order also requires federal officials to cancel any remaining advertising placements, including commercials scheduled to air Sunday evening. The ruling followed a lawsuit filed by Common Cause, a government watchdog organisation, alongside a labour union, its political action committee and an Alabama state legislative candidate. The plaintiffs argued that the administration had improperly diverted taxpayer money towards advertisements designed to promote Trump and influence the political environment ahead of the November 3 congressional elections. The Department of Homeland Security had allocated $20 million for the advertising campaign, which featured the president and highlighted his administration's policies and achievements. The money came from funds Congress had appropriated for immigration enforcement activities. The advertisements began appearing on television in September. It immediately drew criticism from Democrats and government accountability groups over whether federal funds could legally be used to promote the president's political image. The plaintiffs maintained that the campaign violated restrictions on using appropriated federal money for publicity or propaganda. In granting temporary relief, Rochon directed the administration to cancel existing advertising arrangements and refrain from entering into new agreements involving the disputed commercials. The order does not constitute a final ruling on whether the advertisements violated federal law. The underlying litigation will continue. The Justice Department had opposed the request for emergency judicial intervention, arguing that the advertising campaign was already scheduled to end on Sunday. In a court filing, government lawyers said the Department of Homeland Security had no plans to purchase additional advertising time for the campaign. The administration also challenged the plaintiffs' legal standing to bring the case and questioned whether the dispute justified immediate court intervention. The White House has defended the advertisements as public service announcements intended to inform Americans about government policies and accomplishments. Administration officials have argued that previous presidents from both major political parties used public funds to communicate their policy priorities. Trump had earlier said that future advertisements would be financed through his political action committee rather than taxpayer funds, although he did not commit to reimbursing the government for money already spent. The ruling was welcomed by the organisations challenging the campaign. "We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda," the coalition said in a statement released by Democracy Forward, one of the organisations representing the plaintiffs. The coalition argued that government resources should not be used to influence electoral outcomes. The New York case is one of several legal challenges brought against the advertising campaign. The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the administration in Washington, alleging that the advertisements violated federal spending restrictions and disadvantaged Democratic candidates ahead of the midterm elections. The DNC filed its lawsuit on October 7 and subsequently sought emergency relief to stop additional government-funded broadcasts. The controversy comes as Republicans and Democrats prepare for the November 3 midterm elections, when control of Congress will be contested. Although Trump is not on the ballot, the results will determine the balance of legislative power during the remainder of his presidency.

news.title: Elon and the Rest
news.text:
One man stands head and shoulders above his competition.

Imagine being a 25-year-old, 6’5” guy who goes by the local park. There you see eight-year-old kids playing basketball. You ask if you can join, and they readily agree. Then you dominate. You score at will. You block any shot that they dare put up. In short, you are unstoppable.

It would seem that this analogy applies to Elon Musk. When he joined Tesla, it was common wisdom that nobody could set up a new car company. Some, like DeLorean, tried, but they all failed. There was Mercedes, Fiat, GM, Ford, etc., and that was it. You could try something, but it would either fail or be gobbled up by the big guys for pennies on the dollar. Then came Tesla. Tesla’s current market capitalization of nearly $1.5 trillion is more than 10 times that of the “Big Three” combined. And Musk was not the son of Lee Iacocca or some car engineer who wanted to prove others wrong. He showed up out of the blue, made and makes incredible cars, and is leading the world in driverless vehicles with Robotaxis poised to supplant the traditional cab and Uber business models.

And Musk seems to be like this in every field he enters. When our kids were young, I showed them the Tintin color cartoon videos. They were clean, they were high-quality, and most importantly, our kids learned English from them. In one of Hergé’s books and the subsequent movie, Tintin’s friend Calculus takes a rocket to the moon. In the video, the rocket lands very nicely upright on the moon. I said that was dumb and explained to the kids about disposable boosters, capsule, lunar lander, etc. I am not worth a trillion dollars. Maybe Musk saw the same thing as a kid and said, “That’s a great idea. Point noted.” He was the first to land rocket boosters upright, and he is still the only one to catch them in the air. He has run circles around NASA, Boeing, and others who seem to have never left the cocoon of Apollo success from the 1970s.

In every field and during every period, there have been individuals who have stood head and shoulders above their peers. In Madrid, there was a ball hung over 9 feet in the air to mimic the height of a ball that Ronaldo knocked in with a header. Michael Jordan won six championships, was MVP multiple times, and also was defensive player of the year. Thomas Edison is still the benchmark for patents and inventions in multiple key fields. There are simply people who are much better than those around them, and it oftentimes isn’t even close. When I was a kid, I was enamored with Vida Blue. At just 21 years of age, he accomplished the following:

24-8 record

312 innings pitched

301 strikeouts

24 complete games

AL MVP and Cy Young Winner

Just for a smidgen of comparison: in 2026, in the entire Major League Baseball, there were 21 complete games, while the strikeout leader had 252.

One of the many amazing aspects of Elon Musk is that he doesn’t use his towering superiority in his fields of endeavor in order to crush his competition. Just the opposite. He has mentioned on several occasions that his patents for Tesla are free for use by competitors. He wants better rockets and better self-driving cars, so he lets others use his company's advances. It has been reported that he slept on the floor in Washington during his DOGE work and did the same at some of his factories. He has a trailer where he apparently sleeps on site when he is at SpaceX. The anti-Musk would be living it big with a fleet of planes and a yacht that stretches from Boston to New York. He would be suing all of his competitors for patent infringement and looking for ways to knock them out of business. Musk is a rare bird, one that comes along once in every couple of generations. Sure, he is wealthy, but his wealth does not seem to have gotten to his head. He has business and humanity goals, and he seems totally focused on them. As “Mr. Wonderful” said, Elon Musk is 100 percent signal and 0 percent noise.

We should celebrate Musk’s great accomplishments. His cars have generated millions of miles of hands-free driving data. His engineers are making better algorithms for even greater success in self-driving. Like Steve Jobs wanting “only 1 percent” of the market with the original iPhone rollout, Musk is starting his Robotaxis in a few markets before he takes over the hired car business. His rockets will be taking off on daily or even hourly schedules. SpaceX will completely revolutionize human space activities, something not seen since NASA sent astronauts to the moon. The US government is streamlining its permitting in light of Musk’s plans, which in turn is allowing Musk to modify his rockets to make frequent launches more feasible. Watching Starlink satellites pop out of his most recent Starship launch is like living a hundred years forward.

One could easily and correctly make a similar argument about Donald Trump. At 80, he seems to need no sleep. He returns late to the White House from rallies or international trips and starts his formal day at 8 the next morning. He could have retired after 2020 and the Biden DOJ would have left him alone. He chose to run again, was shot at, arrested, had his house ransacked by the FBI, and was dragged through four different court cases. Yet, here he is once again as president, kicking the Chinese out of the Americas, pushing Iran to the brink of destruction, and directing America towards a new economic golden age. Biden was barely there, while Obama caved to America’s enemies and made its health system worse and more expensive. Donald Trump and his secretaries are pointing the US towards 250 years of success and international leadership. Look at Marco Rubio’s speech in Athens. That is the venue for the leader of the modern Western world.

Margaret Thatcher once gave a famous speech in Parliament in which she noted that as the rich got richer, everyone — including the poor — also went up in net worth. She accused her opposition of wanting the rich to be poorer via taxes and, in the process, the poor would also become poorer. Even if one does not own a Tesla or a Starlink receiver, he benefits from Elon Musk’s actions. Musk has set the standards for his fields of endeavor. Waymo looks 19th-century with its multiple Lidar systems. Musk took a bet and went with cameras and software. Right now, his Robotaxis are winning, and the millions of miles of FSD (Full Self-Driving) on Tesla cars are helping to improve algorithms and object identification in all light and weather conditions. How would you like to be a Boeing executive in front of Congress, describing how they were going to let a first rocket stage land in the ocean? “Why can’t you do like Musk and save us money?” When Starlink adds phone service to its WiFi service for access anywhere on the globe, I might become their next new customer.

Many people are jealous of Elon Musk, while others hate him for his politics/social views. I think that we should appreciate his accomplishments and vision. When some company says that it will have a new product by 2030, I add five years. When Musk says it, I circle the date on the calendar. Musk knows what he wants and can achieve, and then goes about getting the job done. How quickly did he get Grok up as the best AI (or SI) app? Good on Elon Musk.

news.title: Christopher Columbus Deserves a National Holiday
news.text:
In 2020, in the aftermath of the death of George Floyd, leftists went on a rampage nationwide. One of their favorite targets was Christopher Columbus, the Italian explorer who bravely crossed the Atlantic Ocean in 1492 and united the Old and New Worlds. Mobs associated with Black Lives Matter, a radical group tied to communism, vandalized, destroyed, or removed at least 33 Christopher Columbus statues in American cities.

In the view of the woke left, Columbus “sparked centuries of colonization, genocide, slavery, and racial oppression, the effects of which can still be measured in modern institutions," the Hill noted. 

Fortunately, President Donald Trump and most Americans see Columbus as a heroic figure who deserves honor. Last Friday, President Trump hosted a “Columbus Day Celebration” at the White House in advance of the federal holiday on October 12.

The Trump administration issued a proclamation to “honor his life of valor, adventure, and ingenuity” and made a “pledge to safeguard his story” and “never allow his legacy to be erased by radical extremists.”

As an example of the president’s commitment to honoring Columbus, he installed a replica of a statue that “rioters” had destroyed in Baltimore on the White House grounds. Protesters tore down the original statue and “threw it into Baltimore Harbor on July 4, 2020.” Although the Columbus statue was too badly damaged to fully restore, the new statue is modeled on the original and includes fragments of the original in its base. 

The president pledged that the “days of plunder are over” and that statues are “back more magnificent than ever.”

Trump understands that Americans are tired of their heroes being demonized, their statues destroyed, and their country's magnificent history being attacked. The Left went too far in 2020, and these measures are a much-needed course correction.

Today, 30 states recognize Columbus Day, while “Other states have either replaced it with Indigenous Peoples Day, recognize both occasions, or don’t make either a state holiday (or) treat it as a normal day.”

In President Trump’s view, Christopher Columbus deserves his own holiday because he was a “legend,” whose “vision, fortitude, and perseverance” set in motion a series of events that culminated in the formation of the United States of America.

Although Columbus believed he was traveling to the Orient, he realized he was embarking on a historic voyage. In his letter to the King and Queen of Spain in 1492, Columbus wrote: “ordained that I should not go by land, the usual way, to the Orient, but by the route of the Occident, by which no one to this day knows for sure that anyone has gone.”

During this expedition, his crew became “tired and scared” for it was “the longest voyage out of the sight of land to that date.” Columbus admonished them that it was “useless to complain.” He pledged that the voyage would continue because “He had come to the Indies, and so had to continue until he found them, with the help of Our Lord.”

Columbus Day is also important to the Italian American community nationwide. It was first celebrated as a national holiday in 1937, though its roots go back further. In 1892, President Benjamin Harrison “issued Proclamation 335, declaring October 21, 1892, the 400th anniversary of Columbus’s voyage, a general holiday.” Harrison described Columbus as “the pioneer of progress and enlightenment.”

Columbus Day parades are held nationwide, including in Manhattan, the “world’s largest celebration of Italian American culture and heritage.” Unfortunately, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani boycotted all the city’s Columbus Day parades, including ones in Queens and Brooklyn.

Mamdani has expressed disdain for Italian Americans and Christopher Columbus for several years. In 2020, Mamdani posted “Take it Down” on social media under a photo of the Columbus statue in Queens. For good measure, Mamdani also flipped off the statue with an obscene hand gesture.

Earlier this year, Mamdani decided not to include “Little Italy” in a “map of immigrant enclaves” throughout New York City. The area was excluded despite its popularity and notoriety as a “nationally recognized historic district.”

Another city that has abandoned recognition of Christopher Columbus is Columbus, Ohio, named after him. In 1955, the people of Genoa, Italy, gave the city a Columbus statue. It stood for 65 years until the woke mob convinced Mayor Andrew Ginther to remove it.

President Trump urged the city to restore the statue. He demanded that “Christopher Columbus be put back into the heart of Columbus, Ohio.” Mayor Ginther responded that the President should stop trying to “divide our country” and claimed that no action could be taken while “The statue is the subject of pending litigation.” He vowed to say nothing while “the matter…is before the court.”

One of the groups legally challenging Mayor Ginther and city officials is the Friends of Christopher Columbus Foundation. They filed a lawsuit in “U.S. District Court in Columbus, calling the removal of the statue illegal and discriminatory.”

The lawsuit calls for the statue to be returned to its former place of honor, at the Columbus City Hall. Currently, Columbus’ far-left administration has the statue “sitting in an unknown storage location.”

This historical revisionism must end; it is un-American. Columbus was a historical figure worthy of recognition. According to Bradley Birzer, a history professor at Hillsdale College, Columbus’ 1492 voyage across the Atlantic was “one of the most important moments in world history.” 

In his first crossing, Columbus reached what is now the Bahamas, Cuba, and Hispaniola. In three subsequent expeditions, Columbus explored what is now Jamaica, Puerto Rico, Trinidad, the South American mainland, and the eastern coast of Central America.

Columbus set the stage for other explorers to develop Latin America and eventually the United States of America. As Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation, noted, “We’re not here if Columbus didn’t do what he did.”

Thus, statues and parades nationwide, along with a holiday in his honor, are more than justified to recognize Christopher Columbus’ incredible legacy.

news.title: Will Arizona Keep Its Fascist Attorney General Kris Mayes in Office?
news.text:
Arizona sadly has one of the most fascist attorneys general currently in office, Democrat Kris Mayes. news.title: Appeal issued after Make-A-Wish mascot goes missing from Trump's Doonbeg resort during Irish Open
news.text: An appeal has been issued for the public’s help to bring home Make-A-Wish's much-loved giant teddy bear, who went missing from the charity’s tent at this year’s Irish Open in Doonbeg. For around 15 years, Hope has been a familiar face at Make-A-Wish events across Ireland, welcoming children and families, offering furry hugs and helping the charity bring hope, strength and happiness to children living with critical medical conditions. Her latest outing was to the Amgen Irish Open held last month at US President Donald Trump's Doonbeg golf resort in Co Clare, where Make-A-Wish Ireland was the official charity partner. Hope was last seen in the Make-A-Wish tent in the Championship Village at the Amgen Irish Open at 7pm on Sunday, September 13. But when staff returned to pack up, she was gone. Standing around five feet tall, with soft blonde fur and brown eyes, Hope was wearing her blue Make-A-Wish T-shirt. The charity , which grants wishes to children living with critical medical conditions, is appealing to spectators, event staff, contractors and volunteers who may have seen her being moved or know where she is now. Susan O’Dwyer, CEO of Make-A-Wish Ireland, said: “Hope has been part of our family for around 15 years. She has travelled all over the country with us, bringing smiles and comforting hugs to children and families, and we really miss her. "At five feet tall, she’s quite hard to overlook. If you were in the Championship Village on Sunday evening and saw Hope being moved, or know where she is now, please get in touch. Even a small detail could help us find her. “To someone else, she might look like a giant teddy bear, but to us she is a much-loved member of the team. We would love to bring Hope home.” The charity is particularly keen to hear from anyone who was near the Make-A-Wish tent after 7pm on Sunday, 13 September, or who helped clear the Championship Village after the tournament. Anyone with photographs or video from that evening is also encouraged to check whether Hope appears in the background. Anyone with information about Hope’s whereabouts is asked to contact Catherine Monaghan on 086 8333365 or Catherine@HarteMedia.ie . news.title: Top NATO commander set to issue warning to Russia over any attack
news.text:
BRUSSELS (AFP) : NATO’s top military commander is expected to deliver a warning to Russia on Monday over the alliance’s ability to counter any attack, as worries grow over the threat from Moscow.

NATO officials have said US General Alexus Grynkewich — the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe — will elaborate his “theory of victory” over any potential attack at a security conference in Warsaw.

The move from the top military commander comes as NATO seeks to send a message to Moscow to halt what Western officials say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine’s backers in the war against Russia.

Fears have grown in recent months that the Kremlin is stepping up its actions after high-profile incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport.

“The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage, which is consistent with and grounded upon the alliance’s deterrence and defence plans,” Colonel Martin O’Donnell, a spokesman for the US general, said last week.

“But given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked,” O’Donnell said, noting the theory sets out a framework to do just that.

NATO — which was founded in the wake of World War II to counter the Soviet Union — traditionally closely guards its defence plans to counter any attack by Russia.

Grynkewich’s intervention looks unlikely to divulge many new details on NATO’s strategy and is intended to both send a signal to Moscow and reassure members on the alliance’s eastern flank.

NATO insists it remains a defensive alliance and has no intention of attacking Russia.

Western officials say that Moscow’s “hybrid attacks” have become more reckless as the Kremlin’s forces are stalled in Ukraine, and that they risk causing significant loss of life.

The alliance — whose primary purpose is deterring an armed Russian invasion — has struggled to work out how to cope with incidents in the grey zone beneath open conflict.

NATO civilian head Mark Rutte has urged countries to keep “calm, carry on and support Ukraine”.

“We should not be naive… about Russia, but they know we are stronger,” Rutte said last month.

But the uptick in Russian activity comes at a time of potential vulnerability for Europe. Allies are currently bracing for possible cuts to US forces in Europe as the Pentagon conducts a review of its deployments on the continent.

The results of the process are expected to be announced towards the end of the year.

European countries are already rushing to bolster their militaries as doubts have soared over the reliability of the United States under President Donald Trump.

news.title: Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads
news.text: President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.“Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements” during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as “rather standard” but, amid backlash, said he would pay for them from his political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow.”.The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested that violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda” and potentially other laws.“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the nonprofit legal organization that represents them. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”In a court declaration Saturday, senior DHS official Holly Mehringer wrote that the money came from funds appropriated by Congress that are “available for, among other things, ‘commemorating efforts and events related to border security.’”The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs..The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration’s capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.The use of public funds to pay for the ads drew heavy criticism — including from some in the GOP."It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters.The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the Republican administration over the ads.Amid the backlash, Trump said he would start paying for the ads with a campaign account. news.title: Gold gains on weaker oil, dollar; US inflation data in focus
news.text:
Gold rose on Monday, supported by a ‌softer dollar and lower oil prices, as investors awaited key US inflation data this week for clues on the Federal Reserve’s next policy move.

Spot gold was up 0.3% at $4,206.01 per ounce, as ​of 0253 GMT, after hitting its highest since October 2 earlier in the ​day. US gold futures for December delivery gained 0.3% to $4,230.40.

“Softer oil ⁠prices on the back of Trump’s reported energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, combined ​with a more subdued dollar, have given gold a window of opportunity to the ​upside to start the week,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

“As oil eases, it takes some of the immediate inflation and interest rate anxiety out of the market, which helps ​gold from a yield perspective.”

US President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement of an energy ​ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday that he said was “effective immediately”, but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr ‌Zelenskiy ⁠said he was still waiting to see details of the deal. Oil prices fell on expectations of more Russian supplies.

The US dollar was muted, making greenback-priced bullion more affordable for buyers holding other currencies.

While gold is typically seen as a hedge against inflation, higher ​interest rates tend to ​diminish non-yielding bullion’s ⁠appeal.

Markets are now awaiting the US Consumer Price Index (CPI) report on Wednesday, followed by the Producer Price Index (PPI) and retail sales ​data on Thursday.

Traders see a 17% chance of a rate hike ​in October ⁠and an 86% probability of an increase by December, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.

Meanwhile, US consumer sentiment slumped further in early October as the rising cost of living because of ⁠the Middle ​East conflict soured households’ views of the economy.

Among ​other metals, spot silver rose 0.5% to $61.12 per ounce, platinum gained 1% to $1,704.70 and palladium climbed 1.2% to $1,161.81.

news.title: Judge Orders White House to Stop Airing Taxpayer-Funded Ads
news.text:
A federal judge on Oct. 11 issued a temporary restraining order barring the White House from airing the remaining slots of taxpayer-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump and his administration’s policies and achievements.

U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon said the motion filed by watchdog group Common Cause, candidate for Alabama State House Robert Hunter, and Service Employees International Union 32BJ and its political action committee had the legal standing to challenge the White House ads.

Rochon barred the administration from “using, disbursing, or transferring funds appropriated to the Department of Homeland Security to develop, create, disseminate, place, distribute, publish, or air the challenged advertisements.”

The judge also ordered the administration to cancel ads scheduled for broadcast on Oct. 11.

The order named the Department of Homeland Security and its chief Markwayne Mullin, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants.

In a statement, the coalition praised the judge’s decision, saying it would help to prevent the use of taxpayer money on what it called “unlawful political propaganda.”

“There is no legal justification—and no precedent—for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda,” it said.

The White House has previously said the ads were not campaign ads, noting that Trump is not on the ballot in the November election.

“These public service announcements are unapologetically American, clearly disclosed, and aimed at the country—not a line on the ballot,” it said in a Sept. 25 statement.

The White House also cited examples of past administrations from both parties using such ads to explain their policies and promote their visions for the nation.
news.summary: The judge also ordered the administration to cancel ads scheduled for broadcast on Oct. 11.

news.title: World leaders, governments condemn attack on Riyadh airport that killed at least 13
news.text:
Leaders and senior officials from across the world have condemned the deadly attack on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed at least 13 people, including an Indian national, and injured more than 300.

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes against Yemen's Houthi rebels, according to US media reports.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney were among those who denounced the attack, while Pakistan, Qatar, Palestine, Jordan and Malaysia expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia.

Saturday's strike, which Saudi Arabia blamed on the Iran-backed Houthis, was the latest in a series of attacks on the kingdom's infrastructure amid an intensifying conflict in Yemen. Saudi airports have come under several attacks this month, including strikes on Riyadh and Abha.

The latest violence comes against the backdrop of the wider war involving Iran and its regional adversaries, raising concerns about further instability across the region.

Von der Leyen said the attack marked a "dangerous escalation," expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its people, and offered condolences to the victims and their families.

She said attacks by Iran's proxies were pushing the region into a spiral of violence and destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.

The EU chief described the attacks on civilians as murderous and said they must stop immediately.

Guterres on Sunday said he was "deeply shocked" by the attack and strongly condemned it. "Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately," the UN chief said in a post on X.

Trump said on Saturday he was considering whether the United States should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he told reporters, according to the AP news agency.

Rubio said the US strongly condemned the recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the strike on Riyadh's airport that killed an American citizen.

"These reprehensible attacks must stop," he said, adding that Washington stood with Saudi Arabia and extended condolences to the victims and their families.

Carney described the Houthi attacks as "abhorrent," saying there could be no justification for attacks on civilian infrastructure or the deliberate targeting of innocent people.

"Canada condemns these reckless acts of violence in the strongest possible terms," he said in a social media post, extending condolences to the families of those killed and wishing a full recovery to the injured.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni strongly condemned the Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport and expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and the families of the victims.

"Attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure are unacceptable and must cease," she said, adding that Italy would continue working with regional partners to reduce tensions and promote stability and freedom of navigation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also condemned what he called the "horrific terrorist attack" on King Khalid International Airport and extended condolences to the families of those killed.

"Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with resolve," Netanyahu said.

He said Israel looked forward to a strong Middle East united against threats and working towards security, cooperation and prosperity.

Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, described strikes on civilian airports in Saudi Arabia as a "grave escalation," warning that they threatened regional security and complicated efforts to achieve peace.

Switzerland condemned the deadly attack and called for immediate de-escalation, urging all parties to respect international humanitarian law, particularly provisions concerning the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure.

Turkish official Burhanettin Duran strongly condemned the attacks targeting civilians and airports in Saudi Arabia, saying the international community needed to adopt a joint and determined stance to prevent the region from being dragged into further conflict and chaos.

Malaysia PM Anwar Ibrahim said he unequivocally denounced the attack, which had taken innocent lives and left hundreds injured. He extended condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a swift recovery.

"There can be no justification for attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure," Anwar said, adding that such attacks could deepen the suffering caused by the conflict and spread it to places that should remain beyond its reach.

Malaysia stood in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and hoped diplomacy and reason would prevail before the conflict widened further, he said.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also strongly condemned the attack, calling it a flagrant violation of international law and a threat to regional peace and stability.

Sharif reaffirmed Islamabad's support for Saudi Arabia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and security, citing the two countries' ties and the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed in August.

The agreement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye on August 7, stipulates that an armed attack against any one of the three countries shall be regarded as an attack against all three.

Qatar's Foreign Ministry condemned the attack as a grave violation of Saudi Arabia's sovereignty and a direct threat to regional security, civilian safety and air navigation. It expressed solidarity with Riyadh and said Saudi Arabia's security was integral to Qatar's own security and that of the Gulf Cooperation Council states.

Palestine's Foreign Ministry condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. It offered condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a speedy recovery.

Egypt also condemned the attacks, describing them as a violation of international law and expressing concern over the threat to civilian safety.

Bangladesh strongly condemned the attack, which killed two of its nationals, and said its mission in Riyadh was in contact with Saudi authorities to obtain details about the Bangladeshi victims and provide necessary assistance to those affected.

Dhaka called for an immediate cessation of hostilities, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure and a peaceful resolution of the crisis through dialogue and diplomacy.

It also reiterated its solidarity with the Saudi government and people.

India on Sunday also strongly condemned repeated attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport over the past few days, including Saturday's strike.

"We strongly condemn the repeated attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport over the past few days, including the dastardly attack on October 10, which have led to loss of lives, injuries and damage to property," the Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement.

Describing the attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure as "completely unacceptable", the ministry said they must cease immediately. It expressed condolences to the families of those killed, wished the injured a speedy recovery and voiced solidarity with the Saudi government and people in defence of the kingdom's sovereignty.

It also expressed hope that peace and normalcy would return to the region soon.

In a separate development, Israeli President Isaac Herzog sent a letter of recognition to Captain Smit Machchhar, praising him as a "hero of Israel, India, and all of humanity".

Herzog said he was praying for Machchhar's full and speedy recovery and invited him to Jerusalem after he regained his strength.

The Israeli President said he would be honoured to present Machchhar with the Israeli Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, which he described as Israel's highest recognition of civilian heroism.

Saudi authorities said 12 people were killed and 309 injured in Saturday's attack, some of them critically. The dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals and one citizen each of the US, Egypt, Jordan, Palestine, Syria and Sudan.

An Indian national was also killed while at least 10 others were among the more than 300 people injured in the attack, the Indian Embassy in Riyadh said on Sunday.

The Indian Embassy, in a social media post, said one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today.

“We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased. We are in touch with the family and will provide all support for ensuring the early repatriation of mortal remains,” it said.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed the rebels for the attack, describing it as a war crime and vowing a firm response.

On Sunday, the Houthis renewed their warning to airlines, airport workers and travellers against using Saudi airports, saying the warning should be taken seriously and that Saudi Arabia bore responsibility for what they described as failed interceptions.

Saudi civil aviation authorities suspended airport operations following the attack, while flights were diverted. Several countries also warned their citizens to avoid the facility.

Published on October 12, 2026

Saturday's attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis. news.title: North Korea fires missiles days after South Korea's hypersonic test
news.text:
SEOUL: North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Monday, South Korea’s military said, marking Pyongyang’s fourth launch in a month and following Seoul’s recent test of a hypersonic missile.

The ballistic missiles, which appeared to be of ​different types, were fired at around 9:20 a.m. local time (0020 GMT) from near Pyongyang, and one type flew ​more than 900 km (559 miles), South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

Earlier, Japan’s coast guard ⁠said North Korea had fired two unidentified projectiles, believed to be ballistic missiles, adding that both appeared ​to have already fallen.

South Korea’s National Security Office convened an emergency meeting, where it condemned the missile launches ​as violations of United Nations Security Council resolutions and urged an immediate stop.

North Korea has been under UN sanctions since 2006, aimed at halting Pyongyang’s development of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles.

The latest launches come at a time when tensions have been ​rising between the two Koreas in recent weeks amid weapons tests by both countries.

Last week, South Korean ​President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test ‌by a ⁠South Korean president.

Monday’s missile launches by North Korea appeared to be “a show of force in response to the successful test launch of our hypersonic missile, as well as an intentional demonstration of missile capabilities,” a spokesperson for South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

North Korea last fired a ballistic missile on October 3, with state ​media KCNA saying it was ​a hypersonic missile tested ⁠under the supervision of leader Kim Jong Un.

The tests followed a border mine blast last month that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul said the landmines had been planted ​by North Korea and demanded an apology, but Pyongyang has dismissed this and ​accused South ⁠Korea of provocation.

Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year, including four in the last month.

The unusually frequent tests indicate Pyongyang wanted to increase its leverage ahead of a potential summit between leader ⁠Kim and ​US President Donald Trump, said Song Seong-jong, a professor at Daejeon ​University in Seoul and a former South Korean Defence Ministry official.

“They definitely need to raise the value of their status before meeting ​Trump,” Song said.

news.title: One dead in new attack on Saudi airport, a day after Houthi strike kills 13
news.text:
DUBAI/RIYADH: One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack ​Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen’s Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

Saudi-led coalition forces in ‌Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh’s international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. Eleven people were wounded in addition to the fatality, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

Coalition forces also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country’s Eastern Province, and a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait had been intercepted.

Emergency alerts were also issued in Abha, in the ​south, early on Monday but the danger had since passed, the Saudi Civil Defense said.

The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis, ​who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores ⁠of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam’s two holiest sites.

A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in.

The ​airport was closed after the attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

Houthis claim responsibility for other attacks

In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attack and said ​the group had also struck the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco.

The Saudi government’s media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on Dammam’s King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that “damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way.”

An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammam told Reuters that around 8:30 p.m. (1730 GMT) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike ​the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave.

Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and ​departures at Dammam airport, the kingdom’s third-largest.

The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. “We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions,” the group said.

Britain’s embassy in Saudi ‌Arabia in a ⁠post on X advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Medina.

US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom.

‘Worse is yet to come,’ Houthis warn

Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.

The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. “Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet ​to come, God willing,” Yemen’s Houthi-run foreign ministry said ​in statements carried by Al Masirah television.

US President ⁠Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.

In a post on Telegram, Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said he told his Saudi counterpart that Tehran was ready to help facilitate ​dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Energy conference still going ahead

A five-day conference of international energy organization WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention ​centre about 10 km (6 miles) from ⁠the Riyadh airport, the Saudi energy ministry said.

A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead, according to a media advisory from the ministry. It was not clear which ministers attended.

Italy’s energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link.

German officials were trying to organise a return flight for economy minister Katherina Reiche. She was supposed to return to Berlin from Riyadh on Monday but the ⁠ministry said it ​appeared likely her flight would be unable to take off.

Separately, Saudi authorities announced that in-person classes at schools in Riyadh would be ​shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday.

Sunday’s attack brought the death toll in attacks on Riyadh’s airport to 18 for the week. In Saturday’s attack, the dead included four Saudis while the remainder were foreign nationals, Saudi authorities said.

news.title: Trump ‘really mad’ with Zelensky – media
news.text:
US President Donald Trump is furious with Vladimir Zelensky over Kiev’s continued attacks on Russian oil refineries, with Washington reportedly threatening to cut off weapons supplies and intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stops the strikes, according to Axios and the Financial Times.

The confrontation comes after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease a global fuel shortage that has sent American energy prices soaring. Kiev has continued targeting Russian refining facilities despite repeated warnings from Washington, with Trump accusing Zelensky of deliberately hurting American consumers and farmers while refusing opportunities to end the conflict.

“Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the US for granted,” a White House official told Axios on Sunday. The source argued that Kiev’s attacks on Russian refineries were doing more damage to its relationship with Washington than to Moscow.

American officials contacted Kiev and several European capitals over the weekend, threatening to suspend intelligence sharing and the NATO-backed Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, through which European countries purchase American weapons for Ukraine, according to the Financial Times, which cited officials familiar with the discussions.

Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also allegedly warned Ukrainian representatives during talks in Miami on Friday that Washington could stop sharing intelligence if Kiev continued to ignore the president’s demands, according to a Ukrainian official cited by Axios.

A US official, however, denied making direct threats, saying the negotiators had instead reminded Kiev of Washington’s extensive military and intelligence support and urged it to stop taking actions that hurt American consumers.

The confrontation has threatened to derail broader negotiations aimed at ending the Ukraine conflict. Witkoff and Kushner have reportedly put their planned trip to Moscow on hold until Kiev and its leading European backers clarify whether they are prepared to support a unified peace proposal.

Trump reached a diesel deal with Putin on Friday after Zelensky ignored at least half a dozen requests from Washington to stop striking Russian refineries, according to earlier Axios reporting. The US Treasury subsequently eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 2027, while Moscow pledged substantial fuel deliveries to help alleviate global shortages.

Zelensky condemned the move as a “weak decision,” arguing that the agreement would provide Russia with additional revenue. Trump hit back by accusing the Ukrainian leader of creating problems for the world and suggesting it was time for Ukraine to elect a new leader capable of reaching a deal.

On Sunday, Trump unexpectedly announced that Moscow and Kiev had agreed to an immediate ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.

The announcement caught Kiev by surprise, with Zelensky saying it “was news for me.” Moscow has also yet to confirm any agreement.

A White House official described the proposed agreement as a “refinery for refinery” arrangement, under which both sides would stop attacking oil refineries, but not necessarily other energy infrastructure, according to Axios. Kiev has objected that such a deal would disproportionately benefit Moscow, since Ukraine has only one largely nonfunctional refinery and relies heavily on imported fuel.

news.title: World News | Death Toll in Migrants' Boat Capsizing Near Djibouti Coast Rises to 139, 84 Still Missing
news.text:
Geneva [Switzerland], October 12 (ANI): The death toll in a migrant boat capsizing off the coast of Djibouti has risen to 139, with 84 people still missing, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said, as search and rescue operations continued following one of the deadliest shipwrecks recorded along the Eastern Migration Route.

In a statement issued on Sunday, the UN migration agency said that the toll rose from 109 to 139 after 30 additional bodies were recovered.

The boat was carrying 305 people from Djibouti towards Yemen when it capsized near Guehere, north of Obock in Djibouti, on the intervening night of October 8 and October 9.

About 82 people survived the disaster, while Djiboutian authorities continued search and recovery operations amid growing fears for those still missing.

Also Read | Donald Trump Claims Russia-Ukraine Energy Ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky Says Deal Is 'News to Me'.

IOM Director General Amy Pope called for urgent action to prevent further migrant deaths and urged governments and donors to expand safe and legal migration options.

"No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," said IOM Director General Amy Pope.

"We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down," she added.

The IOM said it was providing emergency assistance to survivors at its Migrant Response Centre in Obock, including healthcare, psychosocial support, food, shelter and protection services.

The latest tragedy has once again highlighted the dangers faced by migrants travelling along the Eastern Route, which sees tens of thousands of people from the Horn of Africa pass through Djibouti each year in an attempt to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait into Yemen and eventually reach Gulf countries in search of employment, security and stability.

Poverty, regional insecurity and the growing effects of climate change continue to drive people towards the perilous journey, despite the significant risks associated with crossing the sea and the dangers awaiting migrants in Yemen.

According to the IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix, more than 20,000 incoming migrant movements from Ethiopia into Djibouti have been recorded since September 10 alone, underscoring the continued scale of migration along the corridor.

Migrants who reach Yemen face further risks, including violence, arbitrary arrest, detention, exploitation and human trafficking, adding to the humanitarian challenges in the country.

Fatalities and disappearances along the route have continued to mount. The IOM's Missing Migrants Project recorded more than 900 migrant deaths or disappearances along the corridor in 2025, as the overall volume of journeys increased by 18 per cent.

In March 2026, another shipwreck off the coast left nine people dead and 45 missing, highlighting the recurring dangers of the sea crossing.

The IOM said it was working closely with Djiboutian authorities to support rescue operations and prevent migrant deaths on land and at sea. However, the agency warned that expanding humanitarian needs were outstripping the limited funding available.

The organisation called on international donors and partners to urgently strengthen support for Djibouti's search and rescue response and pressed for expanded safe migration pathways to reduce the risks faced by people undertaking these dangerous journeys. (ANI)

news.title: US judge blocks taxpayer-funded Trump ads
news.text:
Washington, Oct 12 (SocialNews.XYZ) A federal judge has ordered President Donald Trump's administration to immediately stop airing taxpayer-funded television advertisements promoting President Donald Trump, handing a legal victory to groups challenging the use of government money for political messaging weeks before the November midterm elections.

US District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York on Sunday (local time) issued a temporary restraining order barring the administration from developing, placing or broadcasting the disputed advertisements for 14 days.

The order also requires federal officials to cancel any remaining advertising placements, including commercials scheduled to air Sunday evening.

The ruling followed a lawsuit filed by Common Cause, a government watchdog organisation, alongside a labour union, its political action committee and an Alabama state legislative candidate.

The plaintiffs argued that the administration had improperly diverted taxpayer money towards advertisements designed to promote Trump and influence the political environment ahead of the November 3 congressional elections.

The Department of Homeland Security had allocated $20 million for the advertising campaign, which featured the president and highlighted his administration's policies and achievements.

The money came from funds Congress had appropriated for immigration enforcement activities.

The advertisements began appearing on television in September. It immediately drew criticism from Democrats and government accountability groups over whether federal funds could legally be used to promote the president's political image.

The plaintiffs maintained that the campaign violated restrictions on using appropriated federal money for publicity or propaganda.

In granting temporary relief, Rochon directed the administration to cancel existing advertising arrangements and refrain from entering into new agreements involving the disputed commercials.

The order does not constitute a final ruling on whether the advertisements violated federal law. The underlying litigation will continue.

The Justice Department had opposed the request for emergency judicial intervention, arguing that the advertising campaign was already scheduled to end on Sunday.

In a court filing, government lawyers said the Department of Homeland Security had no plans to purchase additional advertising time for the campaign.

The administration also challenged the plaintiffs' legal standing to bring the case and questioned whether the dispute justified immediate court intervention.

The White House has defended the advertisements as public service announcements intended to inform Americans about government policies and accomplishments.

Administration officials have argued that previous presidents from both major political parties used public funds to communicate their policy priorities.

Trump had earlier said that future advertisements would be financed through his political action committee rather than taxpayer funds, although he did not commit to reimbursing the government for money already spent.

The ruling was welcomed by the organisations challenging the campaign.

"We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda," the coalition said in a statement released by Democracy Forward, one of the organisations representing the plaintiffs.

The coalition argued that government resources should not be used to influence electoral outcomes.

The New York case is one of several legal challenges brought against the advertising campaign.

The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the administration in Washington, alleging that the advertisements violated federal spending restrictions and disadvantaged Democratic candidates ahead of the midterm elections.

The DNC filed its lawsuit on October 7 and subsequently sought emergency relief to stop additional government-funded broadcasts.

The controversy comes as Republicans and Democrats prepare for the November 3 midterm elections, when control of Congress will be contested. Although Trump is not on the ballot, the results will determine the balance of legislative power during the remainder of his presidency.

Graham’s Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 that Mr Trump signed off on which, if applied, could see the US levy a tariff of up to 100 per cent on countries like India and China that have been buying Russian oil and gas. It is clear Mr Trump will sacrifice any principle at the altar of convenience to try and protect the slender majority his party enjoys in the US Senate and House of Representatives when a third of their seats go to the midterm polls on November 3. That he would speak to one of the US’s biggest rivals to plead for three lakh tonnes of diesel so domestic prices can be brought down before the elections lays his action open to ridicule. India was the big scapegoat against which Mr Trump wielded the big stick as he rewrote the regulations for new H-1B visas, armed his administration to levy fees of $1,00,000 on students and suspended mostly Indian IT companies from the PERM (program electronic review management) to stop the route to getting US green cards for employees. And now he is to buy diesel after berating China and India for buying Russian energy and so funding the war on Ukraine. Republican lawmakers are talking of a bipartisan bill to block the move to lift sanctions on Russian diesel. This may be symbolic but points to the kind of contradictions that a whimsical President is prepared to rain down on his nation as he yo-yos from one position to its exact opposite while grappling with the effects of the war on Iran that he began at Israel’s behest. So embarrassing is a deal with Russia at a time when it is attacking the Ukrainian capital and other cities with renewed vigour and is threatening Europe with military action that it militates against any clear American thinking on strategic geopolitics. And Mr Trump has the effrontery to rebuke Ukraine for striking at Russian oil refineries while calling for Volodymyr Zelenskiy to be replaced as its President. Far from saving the world from wars, the Nobel Peace Prize wannabe is just opening more avenues for escalating conflicts.

news.text:
Indian shares are set to open higher on Monday after snapping their longest weekly losing run in 25 years on Friday, as oil prices fell on expectations of a ​Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire and the central bank unveiled new currency-support measures.

GIFT Nifty ‌futures were at 22,624.5 at 7:53 a.m. IST, indicating a positive start for the Nifty 50, which closed at 22,520.45 on Friday.

Brent crude futures fell 1.6% to $103 a barrel, after US President Donald Trump said Ukraine ​and Russia had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy facilities following ​a US diesel-supply deal with Moscow, easing immediate supply pressure.

However, the Middle East ⁠conflict kept crude above $100 a barrel, keeping sentiment capped.

Over the weekend, the Reserve Bank ​of India unveiled fresh measures to shore up the rupee, redirecting oil companies’ dollar purchases away ​from the spot market and tightening hedging rules as the currency hovers near record lows.

The RBI’s steps to curb spot-dollar demand and support the rupee ease currency volatility, helping temper inflation and foreign outflows—both positives for ​equity-market sentiment.

“The recent rebound after an eight-week losing streak is encouraging, but not sufficient to ​confirm a sustained recovery, and at this stage, it appears more like a relief rally,” said Pabitro ‌Mukherjee, deputy ⁠vice president of research at Bajaj Broking.

The Nifty and Sensex rose 0.4% and 0.8% last week, helped by upbeat quarterly updates from financials and a rise in IT company Tata Consultancy Services as the software firm’s earnings underscored growing AI-related revenue contribution.

“Market needs stronger price action ​and supportive macroeconomic developments ​to establish a durable ⁠uptrend,” Mukherjee said.

Foreign portfolio investors offloaded domestic stocks for 11 straight sessions, with outflows of 35.69 billion Indian rupees on Friday.

Domestic institutional investors ​bought shares worth a net 47.43 billion rupees ($490.18 million), as per ​NSE’s provisional data.
