news.title: Trump's diesel deal not expected to lower prices
news.text:
US President Donald Trump says a new deal with Russia will lower diesel prices, but experts say it won't "move the dial" on costs for consumers.

Mr Trump is also being criticised for forging an agreement that defies his country's stance on depriving Russia of income to fund its war against Ukraine.

Here's what we know about the deal and the impact it could have.

What's in this new deal?

Diesel prices have reached near-record highs in the US, sparking concern in highly reliant sectors such as agriculture and transport.

Mr Trump announced on the weekend he had brokered a deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, which would see Moscow supply diesel "to the American and global marketplace".

He said this would include:

272,000 tonnes "immediately"; then454,000 tonnes next month; then907,000 tonnes "immediately thereafter"; and then2.72 million tons "within a short period of time"

Here's the exact wording to Mr Trump's "very big and important announcement":

Shortly afterwards, the Russian government said it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports, which it announced in July after Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries.

Kyiv and Moscow have been targeting each other's critical energy infrastructure.

Before the weekend was out, Mr Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia would begin immediately, without elaborating on the details.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later said the ceasefire was "news to me" but he supported it if Russia stopped striking energy targets.

However, he said Russian attacks had continued despite Mr Trump's announcement.

There was no immediate comment from the Russian government.

Will the deal lower diesel prices?

Analysts don't think it'll make much of a difference in the long run.

Diesel prices are high due to Russia and China halting international diesel exports to sure up their domestic supply, the ongoing war in Iran, and attacks on energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

International Energy Agency executive director Fatih Birol has said the conditions "merit immediate attention".

Dr Birol called for members to speed up the delivery of their planned exports and consider increasing the amount they're exporting.

Ron Bousso, an energy columnist for news syndicate Reuters, told ABC Radio National the deal would not have a large effect on prices.

"If you put together all the numbers that Donald Trump said Russia would supply, it totals 12 hours of global supply," Mr Bousso said

However, he says the energy ceasefire could be more effective.

"The energy ceasefire could, in theory, change the picture, although repairing a lot of those refineries would probably take months anyhow," Mr Russo said.

"So again, we're not talking about anything immediate."

Why make the deal?

The US mid-term elections are coming up. While they won't end in the election of a new president, they could see Mr Trump's Republican Party losing seats, which would make it much more difficult for him to pass laws.

With high diesel prices driving up the cost of essentials, this could turn voters against Republicans.

"We see from polls that American voters are extremely worried about the cost of living," Mr Bousso said.

"And Trump is well aware of that."

When Mr Trump announced the deal, he said it would see diesel prices drop "fast".

And while some experts don't think this would be the case, Mr Trump could use the deal to spruik his efforts to cut the cost of living to woo voters.

Backlash within Republican ranks

Mr Trump's deal has attracted criticism from some Republicans, including his former vice-president, Mike Pence.

Only last month, Mr Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill into law, calling it the Lindsey ⁠O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, to honour the Republican who died earlier this year.

Mr Pence said the deal made no sense and would be a betrayal of Mr Graham's legacy.

"Instead of implementing the tough sanctions Lindsey Graham fought to his last breath to enact, President Trump has announced the United States is lifting sanctions on Russian energy, fuelling Putin's war machine," he said on X.

"President Trump should rescind this deal immediately and return to the strong policies of our four years in the White House [and] impose harsh sanctions on any nation purchasing Russian energy …"

Four other Republican senators, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curti, joined three Democrats to issue a statement rebuking the president over the deal.

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," they said.

"The Administration must immediately reverse course."

Retiring Republican politician Don Bacon said: "Propping up Putin's war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities."

'Conflicting messages'

William Taylor, the former US ambassador to Ukraine, told ABC News Breakfast Mr Trump would violate laws with this diesel deal.

"There are laws that were put in place when the Russians first invaded Ukraine, and then when they invaded again in 2022," Mr Taylor said.

"And these laws are meant to put pressure on Putin.

"President Trump wants to end this war but he also wants to bring down the price of fuel.

"So President Trump has conflicting messages and conflicting incentives."

news.summary: US President Donald Trump says his deal with Russia will drive down the cost of fuel but experts say it's effect will be minimal.

news.title: Claude's fake murder tip-off speaks to 'carelessness' of AI companies, expert says
news.text:
An artificial intelligence (AI) model submitted a false murder tip to US police in the latest incident of rogue chatbot behaviour.

Anthropic's Claude communicated the bogus tip to Philadelphia authorities despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive.

While the breach was discovered on September 28, authorities weren't notified for another nine days. 

It has left the White House and experts demanding more transparency, with one arguing the sector needs to prove it is capable of "basic cybersecurity".

Here's what we know so far. 

How did this happen? 

The event occurred on July 18, with a submission made to the official website, PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com. 

The tip purported to have come from someone who might have information about the case, according to a Philadelphia police statement.

It was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to police for investigation.

There was "no indication" the chatbot accessed police data, the statement added. 

Police were then notified by Anthropic about the tip before the company released a statement on October 8.

Anthropic said it discovered the false claim on September 28.

In its statement, Anthropic said Claude Haiku 4.5 had been performing tasks "on randomly selected webpages" but not actively "trying to mislead anyone". 

The tip-off from Claude read as follows, according to Anthropic: 

"I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant."

The chatbot left the name and contact fields empty and submitted.

It was instructed to never "submit anything" destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions. 

Following the police statement, Anthropic said it reported the tip-off "as soon as our technical review was complete". 

It said it had since updated Claude's guardrails. 

What are White House officials saying?

Anthropic contacted Donald Trump's recently formed AI task force, called the Super Intelligence Force, about the event.

US Federal Trade Commission Director of Public Affairs Joe Gabriel Simonson said the new task force expected "immediate and full transparency to the entities involved and the public". 

"We expect Anthropic and all companies to honor their obligations, immediately report incidents, fully cooperate with federal and state law enforcement authorities, remedy any damage, and implement concrete safeguards to ensure these failures do not reoccur," he said on X, matching a task force statement shared to Axios. 

"Our message to all SI [Super Intelligence] companies is clear: delayed notification, inadequate corrective action, and a failure to take responsibility will not be tolerated."

The Philadelphia police department said all tip-offs were vetted by a human but that "unsolved cases involve real victims" and "grieving families".

"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," it said.

"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable."

Failures are 'fundamental', expert says

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese late last month revealed an OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian Medicare data portal earlier this year, as well as NSW government websites.

University of New South Wales AI Institute chief scientist Toby Walsh said the Anthropic tip-off showed OpenAI was not alone, calling it "incompetency" on the industry's part. 

"The failures are again fundamental," he said. 

"Why did Anthropic not have basic oversight of what their agents were doing? Why did Anthropic give their agents more than minimal permissions to do their assigned tasks? 

"This is basic stuff. You only give an agent the minimal permissions needed to do their task. Why then did it have permission to submit a police report?" 

Professor Walsh said it spoke "to the carelessness of the AI companies" as he urged for independent oversight "with teeth".

"But not for the reasons that they feared, that the models would become too capable, but because the companies and the people within them proved incapable of performing basic cybersecurity."

Seyedali Mirjalili, a professor of AI at Torrens University Australia, said it showed the systems were becoming so complex that even "developers struggle to predict their behaviour".

That could mean a "harmless goal" didn't necessarily "guarantee harmless behaviour".

"Even when an AI system's goal is harmless or beneficial, its actions can cross ethical and legal red lines," he said.

"An agent gathering information or completing a test can gain unauthorised access to a service or submit fabricated information to authorities."

Professor Mirjalili called for the sector to be more "proactive" in auditing systems, with clear deadlines for notifying authorities and those affected.

"As AI systems become more autonomous, we need to be clear about who remains responsible when something goes wrong," Professor Mirjalili said.

"The companies developing and deploying these systems are still responsible for testing them, monitoring their actions and reporting serious incidents.

How is Australia regulating AI?

Digital Rights Watch head of policy Tom Sulston said the false tip-off came about because "Anthropic were failing to follow good software development practices by testing their agents on the public internet".

"It's not acceptable for AI corporations to release untested code out into the world where it can cause all sorts of problems for other people," he said.

He said the AI sector needed to demonstrate it was "responsible corporate citizens".

"We have plenty of evidence that they're taking shortcuts around the reliability and safety of their products, so it's important that we're able to hold them to account for these failings," Mr Sulston said.

"We need the Australian government to adopt mandatory AI standards that require Big Tech to disclose which datasets they use to train their AI systems so the relevant regulators can enforce Australian copyright, safety, and privacy laws.

"We also need AI corporations to follow standards around mandatory reporting of failures, as well as demonstrating adherence to good software development practices."

The federal government is currently finalising plans to regulate AI, which could make companies prove they are properly testing models.
news.summary: Questions arise after US police were kept in dark about an AI chatbot's false murder tip-off.

news.title: Shares cautious in Asia as earnings loom, oil slips
news.text:
SYDNEY: Asian share markets got off to a cautious start on Monday as earnings season loomed as a challenge ​to sky-high tech valuations, while oil was choppy after strikes on shipping and airports in the Gulf.

There was considerable confusion about President Donald ‌Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, which neither side had confirmed.

Trump’s proposal for Russia to increase its exports of diesel was also under fire from Republican and Democratic senators as potentially illegal.

Brent futures started higher but soon slipped 1.1% to $103.50 a barrel, away from the recent top of $109.97, while US crude ​futures lost 1.2% to $90.73 a barrel.

South Korean stocks fell 1.1%, while MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was little ​changed.

On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures edged up 0.2%, while Nasdaq futures firmed 0.5%. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 ⁠futures firmed 0.4%, while DAX futures gained 0.4% and FTSE futures added 0.3%.

Trade was thin with Japan markets shut and the US on a ​partial holiday ahead of the earnings season with major US banks kicking off on Tuesday.

S&P 500 earnings are expected to have jumped by more than ​30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, though the bulk of that comes from the tech sector.

My Bui, an economist at AMP, noted all the gains in the S&P 500 since mid-September had been in tech, while investors were demanding higher yields to fund the massive borrowing for AI.

The US investment-grade credit default ​swap index, which tracks the cost of insurance against default, had also risen sharply to its highest level since the Iran war began.

“Overall, wider ​spreads suggest investors are questioning whether AI revenues can keep pace with rising borrowing costs,” added Bui. “Corporate bond issuance to fund AI capex, combined with wider ‌high-yield spreads, ⁠will raise refinancing costs as the current wave of debt matures over the next few years.”

US CPI to heat up, but core cooler

The flood of corporate debt has added to pressure in sovereign markets, driving Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week and lifting the discount applied to company earnings.

The market faces fresh challenges this week from US data on consumer and producer prices and retail sales. Rising energy costs are expected to ​lift CPI by a hefty 0.6% ​to an annual 3.7%, though ⁠the core is seen cooler at 0.2% and 2.5%.

“Oil prices remain higher than we had assumed as shipping costs have soared, and product prices are even higher,” said Bruce Kasman, head of global economics at JPMorgan.

“The ​signals on inflation point to a sharp rebound in headline inflation that will squeeze purchasing power and ​a firming in core ⁠inflation that will keep central banks focused on near-term hikes.”

Markets imply only an 18% chance of a rate rise from the Federal Reserve this month, but an 85% chance of a hike in December. Investors are also wagering on hikes in the EU, Japan and UK before year end.

In currency markets, ⁠the euro remained ​on the defensive at $1.1201 having fallen for five weeks straight amid concerns about government ​deficits in Europe.

The dollar index held near 17-month highs at 102.25 , but has stalled on the yen at 158.15 as the threat of Japanese intervention deters speculators for now.

In commodity ​markets, non-interest-bearing gold rose 0.3% to $4,206 an ounce , having managed to bounce more than 1% last week.

news.text: North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles towards its eastern waters on Monday, South Korea’s military said, as Pyongyang continued its weapons testing amid heightened tensions and a prolonged freeze in diplomatic engagement.South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missiles were launched from an area near the North Korean capital, Pyongyang. Japan’s Defence Ministry detected at least two missiles and assessed that they had landed in waters outside the country’s exclusive economic zone.South Korea’s presidential office condemned the repeated launches, saying they violated United Nations Security Council resolutions and urging Pyongyang to stop such activities immediately.The latest launches came days after South Korea flight-tested its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon on Friday. Designed to travel at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defence systems, the weapon was described by President Lee Jae Myung as an important step towards strengthening the country’s conventional defence capabilities.North Korea has intensified its weapons development as leader Kim Jong Un seeks to expand the country’s arsenal of nuclear-capable systems. On October 3, Pyongyang conducted a test of what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to penetrate missile defence systems in South Korea and Japan.The country has also carried out missile tests and live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship, underscoring Kim’s push to strengthen its military capabilities despite repeated US and South Korean offers to resume diplomatic engagement.Tensions on the Korean Peninsula have also been aggravated by a series of land mine explosions near the heavily militarised inter-Korean border last month that injured three South Korean soldiers. South Korea’s military and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that the blasts were caused by mines planted by North Korea. Pyongyang has denied responsibility and dismissed Seoul’s demands for an apology.Kim has halted diplomatic engagement and cooperation with South Korea in recent years, describing the neighbouring country as a permanent enemy. Nuclear negotiations with Washington have also remained stalled since 2019, when talks broke down during US President Donald Trump’s first term.Kim has so far rejected Trump’s overtures to revive dialogue. news.title: Dollar stays near 18-month high as Mideast conflict, inflation data in focus
news.text:
SINGAPORE/SHANGHAI: The dollar held ground near its strongest level in a year and a half in early Asian trade on Monday ​as an escalating Middle East conflict kept investors wary ahead of key US inflation data later this week that will influence monetary ‌policy.

Oil prices swung between gains and losses after Yemen’s Houthis stepped up strikes on Saudi Arabia while two tankers were attacked over the weekend.

Prices were also influenced by Sunday’s announcement from US President Donald Trump about an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. Brent crude futures were down 1% at $103.55 per barrel in Asian hours.

The dollar index , ​which measures the greenback’s strength against a basket of six currencies, was slightly down at 102.14 but remained not far from the 18-month ​peak it scaled last week. Trading was confined to a tight range with Japanese markets shut for a holiday, ⁠thinning liquidity across the region.

“We expect the Houthis to continue their attacks on Saudi Arabian energy assets, supporting gains in the oil price and ​the USD,” analysts at Commonwealth Bank of Australia said in a note.

They added that while Iran had confirmed receiving a US peace proposal through intermediaries, “we ​do not expect a breakthrough this week.”

Against the yen , the US dollar was down 0.14% at 158.160 yen. The Australian dollar and its kiwi counterpart were both roughly flat at $0.6988 and $0.5614, respectively.

Spotlight moves to us inflation data

Beyond the geopolitical backdrop, the market’s focus turns to Wednesday’s US consumer price index report, one of the last major economic releases ​before the Federal Reserve’s late-October meeting on interest rates.

Data last week showed US consumer sentiment slumped further in early October as the rising cost ​of living because of the Middle East conflict soured households’ views of the economy.

The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023 to rein in ‌inflation, with ⁠markets keeping a close watch on economic data to gauge whether policymakers may move again. Traders are pricing in an 81% chance of the Fed standing pat this month, up from 51% a month earlier, CME FedWatch tool showed.

Even otherwise, the dollar’s rally may be due for a pause in the near term with some pullback possible, Barclays analysts said.

They said sharp moves in bond markets had tightened global financial conditions, which could prompt Fed officials ​to strike a more reassuring tone heading ​into the October meeting, particularly ⁠if the CPI reading comes in soft.

Severe selloffs in bond markets in the past few weeks had left investors worried as borrowing costs across the globe rose to multi-decade highs on worries over inflation, energy prices and ballooning ​government debt.

The euro was up nearly 0.1% at $1.121, after clocking a fifth straight week of losses as the ​common currency bore ⁠the brunt of investor angst around France’s fiscal health amid political uncertainty before the 2027 presidential election.

“It is still too early to tell whether higher borrowing costs will be sufficient to impose greater fiscal discipline on the French government,” said OCBC FX strategists.

“We expect EURUSD to consolidate as the intensity of French fiscal ⁠and political headlines ​is unlikely to be sustained,” they said in a note, adding any rally in ​the euro is likely to be capped by Europe’s structural challenges.

The British pound was little changed at $1.3245. Against the Chinese yuan , the US dollar was flat at 6.6927 yuan in offshore ​trade.

In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin rose 0.2% to $83,788.50, while ether edged 0.15% up to $2,540.08.

news.text: The Strait of Hormuz remains on edge as fresh attacks on ships deepen the deadlock over efforts to ease the US-Iran conflict.At least five incidents involving attacks on ships have been reported over the past three days, raising fresh concerns over maritime security along a critical global energy route.According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a tanker transiting outbound was struck on its port side by an unidentified projectile, as reported by the vessel's Company Security Officer (CSO). Before the conflict escalated in late February 2026, the passage carried approximately one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, making it vital to international energy markets.On Saturday, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) forces disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after the ship's crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran.ALSO READ: Russia, Ukraine Agree To 'Energy Ceasefire', Says Donald Trump"A US military fighter jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision munition, fully disabling the ship's propulsion without harming the crew. The large cargo vessel was attempting to transit regional waters after having previously departed an Iranian port," said CENTCOM.Meanwhile, Iran has rejected the United States' response to its seven conditions for reopening the strategically important Strait of Hormuz, with officials saying the proposal remains insufficient to resolve the ongoing standoff.Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Washington had accepted some of Tehran's demands, but several key points remained unresolved or unclear. However, the latest exchange has failed to produce a breakthrough, leaving the timeline for reopening the route uncertain.Tehran has also ruled out linking the maritime dispute to broader negotiations over its nuclear programme.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has maintained that the country's immediate priority is regional maritime security and restoring normal traffic through the strategic waterway, rather than engaging in nuclear talks with Washington.Continued disruption could push up oil prices, increase shipping and insurance costs, and affect energy-importing countries, including India, which relies heavily on imported crude oil.Despite ongoing diplomatic engagement, the two sides remain divided over the implementation of Iran's conditions.With Tehran rejecting Washington's response as inadequate, the prospects for an immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz remain uncertain, keeping global energy supplies and commercial shipping under pressure.

news.title: 1 Killed, 11 Injured In Fresh Houthi Missile Strike At Riyadh Airport
news.text: A fresh Houthi strike hit Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, killing one person and wounding 11 others, a day after another deadly attack claimed by the Yemeni group forced authorities to suspend operations there.Saturday's attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theatre of operations for our forces".Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire.Air defences also intercepted a missile nearby, it added.The fresh attack on the airport killed one person -- a Pakistani resident -- and wounded 11 others, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said on X.Authorities have extended the closure of the airport by 24 hours until 2100 GMT on Monday, the tracking site Flightradar24 said on the same platform.AFP journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the Saudi capital on Sunday."The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook," said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the north of the city.The civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east -- which the Houthis also said they had targeted -- a day after the Saudi coalition reported a projectile landing nearby.Shortly afterwards, the coalition reported shooting down a drone, also in the east.It said early on Monday that it had also "intercepted and destroyed" a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.ALSO READ | "Stay Indoors": Advisory Issued After Houthi Strike Kills Indian In Saudi'Full-Fledged War Crime'Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a call with his Saudi counterpart that "insisting on a military approach and disregarding a political solution would further complicate the current situation", Iran's state media reported.He said Tehran was ready to help "initiate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and facilitate the achievement of a political solution", according to official state news agency IRNA.The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on the Riyadh airport -- where three people were also killed on Thursday -- as well as on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.Although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through."Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it's simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves," said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday's attack a "full-fledged war crime" and vowed to "respond decisively".Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen's Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Sunday.A spokesman for the Houthi-run health ministry said on X that one of the strikes killed a civilian and wounded five others.Saturday's attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the "horrific terrorist attack".ALSO READ| Indian Man Killed In Missile Strike On Saudi Airport, 2 Sons In HospitalFour Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 people wounded.The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded the day before.Operations SuspendedWitnesses to Saturday's strike described chaos in the aftermath."Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood," a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP.The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport.Australia condemned the Houthi attacks as "unacceptable" on Monday, having earlier urged its citizens in Saudi Arabia to stay indoors and "shelter in place".Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.Ottawa University's Juneau said the Houthis now "want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them".On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counter-offensive against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route, military sources said Saturday.The Houthis claimed to have repelled them.Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Oil falls on hopes Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire will boost supplies
news.text:
SINGAPORE: Oil prices slipped on Monday on expectations of more Russian supplies after US ‌President Donald Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy facilities following a US diesel-supply deal with Moscow.

Brent crude futures fell $1.54, or 1.47%, to $103.18 a barrel by 0154 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $90.31 a barrel, down $1.54, or 1.68%.

ICE gasoil futures fell 3% to $1,436 per barrel ​after President Trump said on Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US ​and global markets.

Russia would supply another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”, Trump ⁠added. The daily diesel consumption globally is forecast at close to 29 million barrels, according to the International Energy Agency.

Trump also unexpectedly announced ​on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he was still waiting to see details ​of the energy ceasefire while Russia did not comment.

The announcements eased some of the immediate supply pressure, Tim Waterer, KCM Trade chief analyst, said.

“Questions remain over the validity and longevity of any such ceasefire, and without clearer evidence that it will actually hold, the extent of the pullback is likely to stay limited,” he added.

IEA’s ​Executive Director Fatih Birol said on Sunday that all members should assess whether additional diesel releases are necessary and that countries which have not yet fully delivered ​pledged volumes accelerate their remaining releases prioritising diesel.

Crude supported by middle east conflict

However, the Middle East conflict continued to support Brent crude at above $100 a barrel.

The Houthis claimed ‌responsibility ⁠for a Saturday strike on Riyadh’s international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, while Saudi authorities reported that people were injured in a new attack on the airport on Sunday.

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.

In addition, more attacks on ​tankers sailing through the Strait of ​Hormuz have been reported so far ⁠this month, threatening to dampen a recovery in Middle East crude exports seen in September.

A tanker was struck by a drone in the vicinity of Sohar anchorage, Oman, while another was damaged by an unknown projectile while ​transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported over the weekend.

Goldman Sachs raised ​its Brent crude price ⁠forecast for December to $90 a barrel, up from $85 previously, its analysts led by Daan Struyven said in a note.

“We maintain our base case that continued adaptation of Mideast supply will eventually reduce crude oil prices, while potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” the analysts said, estimating a ⁠risk premium ​of just over $20 a barrel.

“We forecast WTI prices, which are unusually low vs Brent ​because of high US-Europe shipping costs, to average $81 in December 2026 and $73 in 2027,” they added.

In the Gulf of Mexico, energy majors Shell, Chevron and BP were seeking to redeploy personnel ​and restore production at their platforms after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday.

news.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles, adding to streak of weapons tests
news.text:
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korea on Monday fired multiple ballistic missiles toward its eastern waters, South Korea’s military said, adding to a recent streak of weapons demonstrations that has heightened tensions during a prolonged freeze in diplomacy.

Jang Do-young, spokesperson of South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, said missiles of various types were fired from an area around the North Korean capital of Pyongyang, where the country’s main airport has been a major launch site in recent years.

Jang said one of the missiles flew more than 900 kilometers (559 miles) before falling into the sea but didn’t comment on the flight details of the other weapons. The joint chiefs didn’t specify how many missiles it detected.

Japan’s Defense Ministry said it detected at least two missiles and that the weapons landed in waters outside the country’s exclusive economic zone. Japan’s prime minister’s office said no damage has been reported.

While maintaining a hard line toward Seoul, North Korea has been ramping up weapons testing as it seeks to expand its arsenal of nuclear-capable systems, including an Oct. 3 test of what the North described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defenses in South Korea and Japan.

North Korea has also conducted other missile tests and live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship as leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons program while rejecting U.S. and South Korean offers to resume long-stalled diplomacy.

The latest launch came days after South Korea on Friday flight-tested its own domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defense systems, which President Lee Jae Myung described as critical in strengthening the South’s conventional defense capabilities. Without directly addressing the growing threat from North Korea, Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theater of operations.”

Jang, the South Korean military official, said the latest North Korean launches likely were intended to advance the country’s missile technologies while also serving as a possible response to South Korea’s hypersonic test. He declined to say whether the military assessed that the North had further tested its hypersonic technologies in the latest launch, saying the event was still being analyzed.

The South’s presidential national security office called for North Korea to “immediately cease” its repeated ballistic launches, which violate U.N. Security Council resolutions against the North and “do not help manage the current situation on the Korean Peninsula.”

Tensions were further worsened after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border. The South’s military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South’s demands for an apology.

Kim in recent years has halted all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and described the neighbor as a permanent enemy during a prolonged stalemate in larger nuclear negotiations with Washington. He has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump’s calls to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearization as a precondition for talks.

news.title: Maduro-linked fugitive nabbed over alleged scheme to cash in on Venezuelans’ basic needs
news.text:
A fugitive accused of getting rich off programs meant to help Venezuelans is now in U.S. custody, facing charges in a sprawling corruption scandal tied to Nicolás Maduro’s regime.

Alvaro Pulido Vargas, 62, was arrested during a Homeland Security Task Force operation and is scheduled to appear Tuesday, Oct. 13, in federal court in South Florida, the Justice Department announced.

The Colombian national faces two criminal cases alleging he helped funnel money from Venezuelan government bribery schemes through U.S. banks to hide illicit profits.

NICOLAS MADURO AND WIFE CILIA FLORES FACE NEW CHARGE OF CONSPIRACY TO TORTURE AMERICANS

A reward poster for Alvaro Pulido Vargas is marked “In Custody” following his arrest. Federal prosecutors accuse him of money laundering tied to Venezuelan government bribery schemes. (United States Attorney’s Office – Southern District of Florida)

“Pulido is charged in two separate, significant money laundering schemes, both using the U.S. financial system to hide the profits from his bribery and greed off the backs of the Venezuelan people,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva.

Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the arrest Sunday on X, accusing Pulido Vargas of exploiting programs meant to provide essential supplies and housing.

“His alleged actions show a blatant disregard to the Venezuelan people by corrupting government programs intended to provide critical food, medicine, and housing for personal enrichment and exploiting the American financial system to do it,” Blanche wrote.

Pulido Vargas, also known as German Enrique Rubio Salas, was charged in 2019 and again in 2021. The Justice Department said he previously was convicted of drug trafficking in Italy in 1997 under that alias.

“For years, DEA and our HSTF partners have pursued Pulido Vargas across borders. Today, that pursuit has brought him to the Southern District of Florida,” DEA Administrator Terrance Cole said.

The newer case centers on approximately $1.6 billion in Venezuelan government contracts to supply food and medicine through CLAP, a government-run distribution program.

OUR ADVERSARIES ARE EVEN USING THE US BANKING SYSTEM. HERE’S HOW THEY GET AWAY WITH IT

Prosecutors say Pulido Vargas and his associates paid bribes to win the contracts, then inflated prices to cover the payoffs and line their own pockets. The alleged scheme ran from approximately July 2015 through at least 2020.

His son, Emmanuel Enrique Rubio Gonzalez, and former Venezuelan state governor Jose Gregorio Vielma-Mora were among four others charged in the case.

NICOLÁS MADURO AND HIS WIFE EXPECTED TO FACE NEW CHARGES RELATED TO ALLEGED TORTURE OF AMERICANS

Prosecutors say Vielma-Mora and a middleman collected roughly $17.3 million in bribes and illicit payments for helping steer government food contracts and other business advantages to the group.

The money allegedly flowed through a web of companies and bank accounts in Antigua, the United Arab Emirates, the United States and elsewhere. The 2021 indictment describes fake contracts and other paperwork allegedly used to make the payments appear legitimate.

Approximately $180 million moved through or into the United States, including accounts in South Florida, according to prosecutors.

“The allegations describe a profound betrayal of the Venezuelan people; corrupting government programs intended to provide critical food, medicine, and housing for personal enrichment,” said U.S. Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones.

MADURO CLAIMS IMMUNITY, ASKS JUDGE TO DISMISS DRUG-TRAFFICKING CHARGES AGAINST HIM AND HIS WIFE

The earlier case centers on an alleged scheme to cash in on a government program meant to build homes for low-income Venezuelans.

Prosecutors charged Pulido Vargas and Maduro ally Alex Nain Saab Moran in 2019, accusing them of using a housing contract to exploit Venezuela’s government-controlled currency exchange system.

NICOLÁS MADURO FLASHES PEACE SIGNS IN FIRST PRISON PHOTOS SINCE US CAPTURE IN CARACAS

People shouting during a celebration in support of Venezuela. Thousands of Venezuelans living in Madrid gathered at Puerta del Sol to celebrate the arrest of President of Venezuela Nicolas Maduro after President of the United States of America Donald Trump announced that US forces had captured Venezuela’s leader after bombing Caracas. (Marcos del Mazo/LightRocket via Getty Images)

The men allegedly submitted false paperwork claiming they had imported goods and building materials that never entered Venezuela, then bribed officials to approve those documents.

Prosecutors say they moved approximately $350 million out of Venezuela through U.S. banks and into overseas accounts they controlled. The alleged scheme ran from approximately November 2011 through at least September 2015.

Pulido Vargas faces five money laundering-related charges in the 2021 case, each carrying a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison. He faces eight additional money laundering-related charges in the 2019 case.

The DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations are investigating the cases through the Homeland Security Task Force initiative.

Blanche pointed to the arrest as a warning to others facing U.S. prosecution.

“No amount of time or distance will stop @TheJusticeDept from working with our federal law enforcement and international partners to pursue these criminals and bring them to justice in an American courtroom,” he wrote.

news.title: India, US And China In The New Great Game
news.text: Merely because one is driving on a plateau does not mean that the road would not have its ups and downs. That’s what Indian and American officials are finding out as they manoeuvre their way around blind curves and potholes on a road described by none other than finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman as being on a “plateau”. Three days after Piyush Goyal, Union minister for commerce, declared that an India-United States trade deal was all “done and dusted”, the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer said the deal was “not imminent”. Before the dust on that kick up had settled US vice-president J.D. Vance declared that American workers in the information technology industries would not be allowed to yield their jobs to “indentured servants”. The external affairs ministry was quick to reject these words as “unwarranted”. Making a point that my recent book, Secession of the Successful: The Flight Out of New India, underscores on Indian diaspora in the US, the MEA spokesman drew attention to the contribution of “highly educated and skilled” Indians to the US economy and innovation ecosystem. I have a chapter titled “Indians in MAGA” that makes this very point. That the Indian diaspora has contributed billions of dollars to the US economy and constitutes an important force in “making America great again” (MAGA). It is a pity that neither the government nor academic economists have estimated the total contribution of the Indian diaspora to the US economy. In response to President Donald Trump’s continued criticism of the trade surplus that India enjoys in its bilateral trade with the US, the point ought to be made that this is more than compensated by the contribution that Indian Americans have made to the US economy. There is little point in a foreign ministry spokesperson decrying “unwarranted” the comments of a US politician. Much more effective would have been an exercise that shows how many trillion dollars Indian Americans have contributed to MAGA. The US is a nation built by immigrants and even today its most advanced industries are being driven by immigrant talent. So playing the anti-immigrant card for short term political gain is not going to help. But that is America’s problem. As for us in India, we need to free ourselves from the dependency syndrome that many among our policy elites and aspirational middle classes have imprisoned themselves in, believing that the US would help us deal with adversaries, with China’s growing power and with high technology, and offer us a free ride to Viksit Bharat. Ain’t gonna happen. President Trump is focused purely on the American interest. That is entirely understandable. After all he was returned to office to “Make America Great Again”. Prime Minister Narendra Modi wrongly imagined that MAGA and MIGA (make India great again) were two hands of the same body. Sure, that view was what underwrote the India-US civil nuclear energy deal and the India-US strategic partnership under President George Bush. But that movie is over. Over the past decade successive US administrations have sent us invoices for partnership. We paid up on some, buying defence equipment, reducing tariffs on some products, cutting off oil purchases from Iran and Venezuela, and so on. Each time a subservient Indian elite fed the ego of a greedy and powerful US elite, they asked for more. Funnily, though, the turning point came when Mr Trump mocked India with a poke in the eye — inviting a Pakistani general for lunch at the White House. Nothing wakes up the Hindutva leadership like a Pakistani. Things have gone downhill since then. Some in Delhi’s policy circles still hope that after the mid-term elections we will meet a friendlier Trump. Some imagine that after Mr Trump’s term is over a new American leadership will revert to the old script. It is now clear that at least some in the policy making circles do not think so. The sober views expressed by external affairs minister S. Jaishankar at the Asia Society in New York suggest there is some rethinking. Perhaps the rethinking has been prompted by an assessment of where the US-China relationship is headed. Going forward it would seem that India will continue to buy some defence equipment or other to make sure that the US share of India’s defence imports does not go below the 10 per cent level where it is now at. India is unlikely to buy any major platform. No fighter jets please. But, for a few dollars more Pentagon and Mr Trump’s billionaire friends will be kept happy. That allows some retired Indian diplomats and policy analysts to remain in play as lobbyists for American arms exporters. The US may even play along with India to keep the four-nation Quad alive. The US secretary of state, Marc Rubio, is expected to be in New Delhi. He may announce that on the sidelines of the G-20 summit in the US this December there would be a Quad summit. That will keep some America enthusiasts busy. But the new “Great Game”, as London’s Financial Times...

news.title: Passenger terminal at Riyadh airport is struck again, a day after 12 were killed
news.text:
A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.

Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. Saturday's missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began, with another 300 people wounded, some critically. The airport was still closed Sunday.

The sharp escalation in the new front in the war threatens to draw in greater US military involvement, as President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no immediate White House comment Sunday.

India's embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday's attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also had been attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.

The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis.

At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz -- along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.

Trump said he planned to speak to the Saudi crown prince

Trump on Saturday also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance.

A US intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month, and the Saudi-led coalition has been trying to seize them back.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the US has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

Sunday's attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.

“There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix; we come out of the ashes all the time,” the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.

He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.

Houthis have targeted Saudi airports, military and oil facilities

Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60 per cent of them women and children.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.

On Sunday, the Houthis claimed the attack on the airport in Dammam as well as attacks on oil and gas facilities in the kingdom's east. They have targeted the Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, every day since Wednesday.

The rebels again warned “all airlines, experts, employees, workers and ?travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our ?forces.” Several international airlines have suspended flights for varying periods.

The dead in the airport attack included several nationalities

Saudi authorities said the dead in Saturday's attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.

The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant for Saudi airline Flynas, identified as Azza Ramzy, according to Egyptian state-run TV.

The Syrian woman was a widowed mother who had been living in Saudi Arabia, relative Nisreen Oweida told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.

Iran can use the Houthis to pressure a key US ally

Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the Iran war's sidelines, but they have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran's most powerful allies. Now, they are helping Iran to pressure a key US ally.

The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognised government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land.

The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels say they have now imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia.

Fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains near the Bab el-Mandeb, a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has attacked ships.

Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group's senior analyst for Yemen, said the Houthi pressure tactics could backfire: “Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign.”

Published on October 12, 2026
news.summary: Saudi authorities report injuries in the latest attack on King Khalid International Airport, affecting terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights

news.title: France's far-left presidential candidate cheers Gen Z school protests
news.text: PARIS — French far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon on Sunday celebrated high school students whose protest movement has shaken France as he called at a campaign rally for lowering the voting age to 16 and an end to selective admission to universities.The fiery anti-capitalist Mélenchon also took aim at U.S. President Donald Trump, NATO and the global financial system, in a sweeping speech to thousands of supporters meant to kick his campaign into high gear for next year's two-round election in April and May.Also Sunday, France's Socialist and allied voters chose European Parliament lawmaker Raphaël Glucksmann as their presidential candidate in a primary election marred by a cyberattack and divisions within the mainstream left.President Emmanuel Macron is finishing his second term and cannot run again, so next year's election will be a turning point for France and Europe. France is the EU's only nuclear power, its second-biggest economy and a linchpin of the shared euro currency zone.At this stage, polls suggest that Mélenchon and center-right candidate Edouard Philippe are behind far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, but ahead of a range of other hopefuls. It remains to be seen if they will maintain their current level of support.The nationwide high school protest movement — over deteriorating school buildings, teacher shortages, and inequalities hurting schools in disadvantaged neighborhoods — has energized young voters, who may prove key to the election outcome.The movement has at times turned violent, and police have made more than 6,600 arrests. Hundreds have been injured, including students, teachers and police.Mélenchon's critics say he and his France Unbowed party are fueling the fire for electoral gain; Mélenchon says his party isn't organizing the movement and wants it to be peaceful.The party invited student protesters to the stage at Sunday's rally in the southern city of Clermont-Ferrand, and Mélenchon said their protest movement shows ''a high level of political and union maturity.''Many protesters are under 18, and Mélenchon — who is 75 and on his fourth presidential run — nodded to that future electorate by proposing to lower the voting age to 16.He denounced the national university admissions platform that has frustrated student protesters, saying selective admissions should be scrapped and knowledge shouldn't be turned into ''merchandise.''More protests are planned Tuesday and next Saturday.The school protests have pushed the government to order urgent hires of substitute teachers and rearrange school schedules to address grievances. Students at the barricades say that's not enough, but the movement has shown young people the power they can wield, and Mélenchon is hoping it translates into higher youth turnout at the ballot box.This movement is ''marking their entry into politics,'' high school librarian Dounia Georgeon told The Associated Press at a protest this week at her school in eastern Paris. The muscular police reaction is likely to have lasting impact on the students and their politics, she said.Mélenchon also reached out Sunday to older voters, calling for lowering the retirement age to 60 from 62. And he reiterated his push to cancel France's staggering debt.He called Trump an ''adversary'' because of his tariffs, and said France should lead a more independent foreign policy.''We're not preparing our children and grandchildren to die for some hazardous operation concocted by NATO,'' he said. His campaign platform says NATO membership is ''against France's interests,'' calls for better dialogue with Russia, and does not mention Ukraine.Also this weekend, Philippe and centrist candidate Gabriel Attal, both former prime ministers appointed by the unpopular Macron, held rallies.

news.title: Saudi Arabia says 1 dead, 11 injured in latest attack on Riyadh airport
news.text:
The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) identified the deceased in Sunday’s attack as a Pakistani resident and said the injured were transferred to several hospitals for medical care.

The strike on terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, occurred a day after a Houthi missile hit the airport, killing 12 people and wounding more than 300, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13.

Following Sunday’s attack, GACA said damage assessments and safety inspections of the airport were under way.

A witness on board a taxiing aircraft at the airport told the Reuters news agency that a projectile struck the tarmac next to several parked planes at about 8:30pm (17:30 GMT) on Sunday, causing a fire.

The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate, where the passengers disembarked and were told to leave.

The Riyadh airport has been struck four times in the past five days. Houthi attacks on King Khalid airport on Thursday killed at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, according to GACA.

The airport has been closed since Saturday’s attack, which was the deadliest in the country since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for the strikes before Sunday’s.

The airport attacks have escalated the war in Yemen and threaten to draw in the US military. US President Donald Trump says he is weighing whether to join the fight against the Houthis.

The escalation puts further pressure on global oil supplies and prices, as well as on commercial shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait off the Yemeni coast, a crucial alternative waterway to the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump had said he intends to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is seeking help against the Houthis, but there were no signs on Sunday that the US president had followed up on his claim.

There are fears that US intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Gulf.

The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been trying to seize them back.

news.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia attacks multiple power plants after Trump energy ceasefire claim
news.text:
Cars burn after a Russian strike on a residential neighbourhood in Kharkiv, where three people were killed on Sunday. A power plant in the north-eastern Ukrainian city was also hit. Photograph: Andrii Marienko/APView image in fullscreenCars burn after a Russian strike on a residential neighbourhood in Kharkiv, where three people were killed on Sunday. A power plant in the north-eastern Ukrainian city was also hit. Photograph: Andrii Marienko/APExplainerUkraine war briefing: Russia attacks multiple power plants after Trump energy ceasefire claimZelenskyy says Ukrainian skies filled with Russian drones after truce claim, which Moscow has yet to confirm, as six killed in strikes. What we know on day 1,692

Russian strikes hit multiple Ukrainian power plants after Donald Trump claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The Ukrainian president said on social media a drone had hit a power plant in Kyiv on Sunday, leading to power outages in the capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on the CHP-5 power plant in the eastern city of Kharkiv, adding:“Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ [drones] all day.”

Trump said earlier that “effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” the US president wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning in Washington, without further details. Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me” and he was seeking further details. Russia has yet to confirm it agreed.

The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine’s key western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission. British prime minister Andy Burnham said a sustained energy ceasefire was “the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets”. French president Emmanuel Macron said Paris supported a “real energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine.

Ukrainian officials said Russian ⁠attacks killed six people ⁠in two Ukrainian ⁠cities ​on Sunday, including a strike ⁠on a grocery store in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, ​where ‌three people died ‌and 20 were ‌injured. Two children were ‌among the injured, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. In a separate ​attack ​in western ​Ukraine, officials ​said ‌a Russian strike ​killed ​three people.

Trump’s energy truce claim came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel while temporarily easing US sanctions, prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney added to the chorus of disapproval after a Sunday call with Zelenskyy, saying the diesel deal “is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe”. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed Zelenskyy “as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom”, while Germany foreign minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin continued to “fully support” him.

Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy when asked about criticism of the Russia diesel deal, saying it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” who would finally settle the war. Zelenskyy pushed back, telling US ABC News on Sunday: “First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader.”

The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times quoted officials in Europe as saying. The US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries, they said.

A Ukrainian ⁠drone killed one ⁠person in Russia’s ⁠border ​Belgorod region on Sunday, ⁠officials said. The operational headquarters ⁠in Belgorod ​region said the drone struck a car on a road ‌near the border. In the ​part of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region ⁠held by Russian ​forces, Moscow-installed ​officials ​said one ​person ‌had been killed ​in ​a Ukrainian attack.

Russia’s military ⁠said it ⁠struck ⁠a logistics ​centre in southern Ukraine’s ⁠Mykolaiv region and a cargo vessel ⁠in the ​Black ‌Sea. The logistics centre in the town ‌of Ternivka was used to ​store military and dual-use cargoes for the ⁠Ukrainian military, the ‌Russian defence ministry ‌claimed on Sunday.

news.title: Trump says Russia, Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire' but Kyiv says attacks continue
news.text:
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it, and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.

Trump's brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!”

Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country “welcomed” the announcement by Trump as “good news for everyone,” Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv.

“Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian shaheds all day today,” he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow. “There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening.”

The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure -- and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”

Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as “weaponising winter.”

Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin “had one answer to all of them -- nyet.' We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world.”

He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the US, and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.

“We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine,” he told ABC's “This Week.”

Trump spars with Zelenskyy

----------------------------------

Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the US

Zelenskyy said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.

“Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections,” he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made.

“With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader,” he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful, and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added.

Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organising one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy's term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in.

The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data centre in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company's facilities in four days.

Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line.

Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of US midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure.

He has sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort.

Ukrainian strike on Russian data centre triggers outages

-----------------------------------------------------------------

The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data centre in Vladimir caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.

“Operations at the data centre have been completely halted. There were no injuries,” said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which updates service availability.

Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that he had to cancel several rides after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.

“I'd press the call button to contact them, but nothing happens,” he said. “There's nothing I can do, so I'm just forced to cancel.”

Igor Mann said he tried to check on an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform, but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a virtual private network did not help. “Nothing worked,” he said.

Another Muscovite, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had a “direct impact” and weren't just about “convenience.”

“It's also about work,” he said, adding that the outages also affected “healthcare, and everything else.”

On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data centre offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. The next day, Ukrainian drones hit the company's major data centre in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, disabling part of the facility, Yandex said.

Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia's artificial intelligence development.

Zaporizhzhia death toll rises to 23

-----------------------------------------

Elsewhere, search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, according to Ivan Fedorov, former regional head and co-chair of the regional defence council.

Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, with eight still hospitalised.

A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday. (AP) SKS
